rows: Mycotoxins are toxic substances produced by some moulds and can contaminate food and feed.
Cereal grains and derived products can be relevant sources for T-2 and HT-2 mycotoxins.
Food businesses should manage chemical-contaminant risks within their food-safety systems.
Legal limits or guidance values can apply to specified mycotoxins and commodities.
Sampling must account for uneven contaminant distribution within a lot.
Validated laboratory methods are needed for reliable concentration measurements.
Processing and cleaning can change mycotoxin concentrations in foods.
Risk assessment combines occurrence data, food consumption and toxicological guidance values.
The presence of mould or a cereal ingredient does not establish the mycotoxin concentration of a product.
Batch-level conclusions require representative sampling, validated analysis, processing and traceability evidence.
Food additives must be authorised for the intended food and conditions of use.
The official public register lists authorised regulated food and feed products for Great Britain.
Authorisation can specify food categories, maximum levels and other conditions.
Businesses remain responsible for ensuring additive use complies with the applicable authorisation.
Ingredients lists should identify additives by functional class and name or E number as required.
Certain additives require additional warnings or labelling information.
Additive purity, specification and supplier information support compliance.
Changes to a formulation should trigger a review of authorisation and labelling.
An E number does not mean an additive is permitted in every food or at every concentration.
Product compliance requires the exact additive, food category, level, specification and current authorisation.
Importers must ensure that imported food complies with applicable food law.
Controls vary by commodity, origin, risk category and whether food is of animal origin.
Specified higher-risk products may have to enter through an appropriately designated border control post.
Official controls can include documentary, identity and physical checks, including sampling.
Import restrictions and special conditions can change in response to risk evidence.
Consignments may require certificates, prior notification and traceability information.
Labelling, allergens, additives and chemical-contaminant rules continue to apply to imported food.
Importers should check current official requirements before dispatch and arrival.
Country of origin or commodity type does not prove that an individual consignment is compliant or unsafe.
Consignment conclusions require current tariff classification, origin, documents, border checks, sampling and release status.
Chemical food-safety risks can arise from contaminants, processing, packaging, the environment or deliberate ingredients.
Food businesses must identify and manage relevant chemical hazards.
Risk assessment considers hazard, exposure, dose-response and uncertainty.
Health-based guidance values can support assessment for some chemicals.
For some genotoxic carcinogens, a threshold without appreciable risk may not be identifiable.
Controls can include supplier assurance, specifications, process management, sampling and testing.
Food-contact materials and packaging must not transfer unsafe levels of substances to food.
New evidence or an incident should trigger review of chemical-hazard controls.
Detection of a chemical does not automatically mean that food presents a health risk.
Risk conclusions require concentration, consumption, toxicology, population and uncertainty evidence.
